overview: Senegal emerged as a separate republic in 1960 after the brief Mali Federation. Its history includes influential arts institutions, public-health research and the work of sustaining democratic government.

periods.title: Independence and Senghor’s presidency
periods.summary: The federation dissolved in 1960; Léopold Sédar Senghor’s presidency was followed by Abdou Diouf in 1981.

periods.title: Political change within the republic
periods.summary: Successive political eras continued within an independent Senegalese state.

periods.title: A further electoral transfer
periods.summary: The 2024 election brought a democratic transfer after serious political tensions.

items.text: Senegal and the former French Sudan briefly formed the Mali Federation, independent from France in June 1960. Senegal withdrew on 20 August. Today’s Senegal and Republic of Mali therefore share part of their independence story, but are separate countries.

The UN’s 2024 regional report records both pre-election tensions and a democratic transfer of power in Senegal. Elections are historical events involving voters, courts, candidates and public argument, not simply a new portrait in a government office.

An attested French writing sample is Senegal’s motto: “Un Peuple - Un But - Une Foi”. It means “One People, One Goal, One Faith”. The presidency explains it as an aspiration to shared national life, unity and purpose.

sections.title: A meal, a canvas and a classroom

items.text: Ceebu jën developed in Saint-Louis fishing communities. Fish, broken rice and seasonal vegetables form its familiar foundation, but recipes vary. A shopping basket might include carrots, cabbage, cassava or okra: a national dish still leaves room for local cooks.

UNESCO’s account describes cooking techniques passed from mothers to daughters and meals often eaten by hand at home. Restaurants commonly provide spoons or forks. Kitchen knowledge is learned through watching, practicing and eating together, rather than only by reading a recipe.

The meal also has manners: the bowl is steadied with the left hand, and rice should not be dropped. The quality of fish and vegetables can express the importance of an occasion or affection for a guest. Hospitality can be deliciously specific.

Artist Iba Ndiaye returned to Dakar at Senghor’s invitation around independence to establish a national fine-arts school. Born in Saint-Louis, he had studied in France. Education and international exchange helped shape modern Senegalese painting alongside older artistic traditions.

Ndiaye’s Tabaski III, painted in 1970, represents the Islamic Feast of Sacrifice in a West African setting. The oil painting is on plywood and measures 1.5 by 2.5 meters. That is a substantial surface on which to bring local experience into an international art conversation.

At Kaffrine in 2022, UNICEF described girls missing school because of menstrual stigma, inadequate toilets and lack of supplies. Private, functional facilities mattered alongside information. Staying in a classroom can depend on what is available down the corridor.

Nogaye and Ndela joined a group of forty-seven young women and men learning to sew reusable menstrual pads. Their ten-day training combined sewing with business skills. Ndela reported 20,900 pads produced for distribution to schools, connecting paid local work with pupils’ needs.

The Institut Pasteur de Dakar manufactures yellow-fever vaccine and conducts disease research. Its work links technicians, laboratory equipment and production facilities with public health across Africa. Senegal’s scientific achievements include making essential materials, not only publishing discoveries.

The institute also tests drinking water and food, while its surveillance network helps detect unusual illness. Scientific work reaches into ordinary meals and clinic visits: a laboratory can investigate things far too small to see in a glass of water.

ending.text: Senegal continues as a republic. The peaceful transfer following the tense 2024 election is one chapter in an ongoing political history, not an ending for its people or institutions.
